beats.role_note: the problem, the context, the stakes — BEFORE the CLI loop
beats.narration_text: SurveyMind sells synthetic survey respondents — AI personas standing in for real humans so researchers can skip recruiting. Fine, if the personas actually think like people. But nothing stops a model from generating Big Five scores that look plausible trait by trait while the relationships BETWEEN traits — the actual structure of a human personality — are quietly wrong. Ship that into a study and every downstream finding is built on a correlation matrix that was never real.

Into Claude: write validate underscore synthetic dot py — load real and synthetic Big Five data, compute the congruence coefficient between their correlation matrices, run a Jennrich test on whether the matrices statistically differ, bootstrap a confidence interval on the similarity, and run a per-trait Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.

props.command:
claude "write validate_synthetic.py:
  load real vs synthetic Big Five CSVs
  congruence coefficient on correlation matrices
  Jennrich test (do matrices differ?)
  bootstrap CI on similarity
  per-trait KS test"

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — the ACTUAL generated code, trimmed to what teaches
beats.narration_text: Read it before trusting it. The congruence coefficient is Tucker's phi — cosine similarity between the two correlation matrices, flattened. Above point-nine-five, the structures agree. The Jennrich test asks the sharper question: are these two matrices statistically distinguishable at all, not just visually close. And the bootstrap resamples the synthetic set a thousand times so the confidence interval isn't a lie built on one lucky draw.

props.title: validate_synthetic.py
props.code:
# validate_synthetic.py — Claude Code output
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

def congruence(r_real, r_syn):
    a, b = r_real.values.flatten(), r_syn.values.flatten()
    return a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))  # Tucker's phi

def bootstrap_ci(real, syn, n=1000):
    scores = [congruence(real.sample(frac=1, replace=True).corr(),
                          syn.sample(frac=1, replace=True).corr())
              for _ in range(n)]
    return np.percentile(scores, [2.5, 97.5])

# Jennrich: are the two correlation matrices statistically distinguishable?
# KS: per-trait, does the real vs synthetic SCORE DISTRIBUTION match?
props.sparkLine: One matrix, one true structure to match.

beats.role_note: OPEN slot → screen recording of the real terminal run
beats.narration_text: Run it against SurveyMind's better synthetic set. Congruence coefficient: point-nine-seven — the correlation structures line up. The Jennrich test can't reject that they're the same matrix. Bootstrap CI sits entirely above point-nine-five. And every trait clears its Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. This is what a synthetic respondent actually replicating human personality structure looks like: PASS.

beats.narration_text: A validator that only ever says pass isn't a validator. Check it: point it at a synthetic set that's actually broken and see if it catches the fake. Into Claude: re-run validate underscore synthetic dot py against the degraded synthetic sample and report every gate.

props.command:
claude "re-run validate_synthetic.py against synthetic_degraded.csv —
report congruence, Jennrich, bootstrap CI, and per-trait KS for every gate"

beats.role_note: OPEN slot → screen recording of the real terminal run
beats.narration_text: Same script, degraded synthetic set. Congruence coefficient drops to point-seven-eight. The Jennrich test rejects: these matrices are statistically different, not a rounding error. Bootstrap CI no longer touches point-nine-five. And three of the five traits fail their KS test outright. The validator catches exactly what it's supposed to catch — a synthetic respondent that looks fine trait by trait but got the relationships between traits wrong.
beats.visual_intent: same screen-recording layout as B04, now showing the degraded run — lower congruence number highlighted, Jennrich significant result in red, bootstrap CI shifted down, KS table with three rows flagged, ending on a red FAIL

beats.narration_text: So the risk was never whether synthetic scores look plausible — they always do. It's whether the correlations between traits match a real human personality's structure. Congruence coefficient, Jennrich, bootstrap, and per-trait KS together catch what eyeballing a distribution never will: a synthetic population that's fluent but structurally fake.
